claims.text: Thermal activation or service exposure induces Mg segregation in non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Mg segregation promotes formation of discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The evolved alloy has a dual-phase microstructure consisting primarily of a solid-solution matrix and discrete intermetallic precipitates.
The Mg-rich precipitates act as localized barriers that modify oxide-scale formation kinetics.
The Mg-rich precipitates enhance corrosion passivation.
Precipitate formation improves high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast homogeneous state.
The initial alloy has a predominantly homogeneous solid-solution microstructure with minimal intermetallic phase formation.
The initial alloy has a density below 6 g/cm³.
Thermal exposure forms Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates along grain boundaries and in interdendritic regions.
Mg atoms are initially distributed homogeneously in the alloy.
Thermally activated Mg diffusion produces metastable Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
Mg-rich phases modify local chemical gradients and increase phase-boundary density.
The additional phase boundaries are preferential sites for nucleation and adhesion of protective oxide films.
Protective oxide-film nucleation at phase boundaries alters ambient corrosion behavior and elevated-temperature oxidation kinetics.
Thermal aging produces a refined microstructure.
Thermal aging produces well-distributed Mg-rich precipitates.
The thermally aged alloy has a lower corrosion current density than the as-cast baseline.
The thermally aged alloy forms more adherent and protective oxides during high-temperature oxidation than the as-cast baseline.
The proposed behavior applies only when treatment initiates metastable phase separation without complete coarsening or loss of mechanical integrity.
